Ἐὰν μέντοιγε χιτῶνα ἔχῃ τις ἕνα, καὶ τοῦτον τὸν
χιτῶνα προφάσει τοῦ ἀπαιτεῖν τὸ ἐμὸν ἐκδύσω, μὴ ἐλεήσας ἐκεῖνον τὸν γυμνὸν,
ἀμφίασιν τοῦ γυμνοῦ ἀφειλόμην. Πολλὰ δὲ τοιαῦτα ἐν ἡμῖν γίνεται, ὅταν
δανείζωμεν, ὅταν προσ οφειλέτας ἔχωμεν. Πολλάκις ὁ ὀφειλέτης ἡμῶν εἰς
ὑπερβολὴν πένεται, μὴ δυνάμενος ἀποδοῦναι· καὶ ἡμεῖς, τὰ σπλάγχνα ἡμῶν
ἀποκλείσαντες, καὶ μὴ βλέποντες, ὅτι γυναῖκα τρέφει, καὶ τέκνα, καὶ μόλις τρέφεται
ἀπὸ τῶν ποριζομένων αὐτῷ ὀλίγων ὀβολῶν, ἀπαιτοῦμεν πικρῶς, ἔσθ' ὅτε καὶ
περισσὰ ἔχοντες παρ' ἑαυτοῖς. Ταῦτα οὖν λέγει ἐγκαλῶν τῷ Ἰὼβ, ὅτι, «Ἀμφίασιν
γυμνῶν ἀφείλου.» Ἴσως δὲ καὶ τὸ μὴ δοῦναι τῷ γυμνῷ ἱμάτιον ἀφαίρεσιν ὀνομά ζει·
ἀποστερητὴς γάρ ἐστι καὶ πλεονέκτης καὶ ὁ μὴ ἐνδύων τὸν γυμνὸν, καὶ ὁ μὴ τρέφων
τὸν ἄρτου δεόμενον. Ἐθαύμασας δέ τινων πρόσωπα. Ἄλλο καὶ τοῦτο ἁμάρτημα·
ἁμάρτημα γὰρ καὶ τὸ θαυμάζειν πρόσ ωπον. Ὁ δεῖνα, ὅτι πλούσιός ἐστι, θαυμάζω
αὐτοῦ τὸ πρόσωπον· τὸν δὲ πένητα καταπατῶ, ἐπειδήπερ ἀξίωμα οὐκ ἔχει. Ἔσται
οὖν σοι ὁ παντοκράτωρ βοηθός. Ὑγιὲς ἐνθάδε δόγμα ὁ Ἐλιφὰζ λέγει· οἴεται γὰρ τὸν
Ἰὼβ διὰ τὰ ἁμαρτήματα πάσχειν, καὶ ὅτι ὑπομείνας κα θαίρεται δι' αὐτοῦ τοῦ
πάσχειν· καὶ καθαιρόμενος, ὥσπερ χρυσὸς ἐν χωνευτηρίῳ, δόκιμος ἀποφαίνεται, πᾶν
τὸ ἀλλότριον ἀποθέμενος, καὶ πάσης κακίας 12.1040 ἀμιγὴς γεγονώς. Φησὶν οὖν, ὅτι,
ἐὰν καὶ σὺ ὑπομεί νῃς τὰ συμβεβηκότα σοι, ἀποδώσει σε καθαρὸν ὥσπερ ἄργυρον
πεπυρωμένον ὁ Θεός· καὶ καθαρὸς γενόμε νος, παῤῥησίαν ἕξεις, ὡς ἀποθέμενος τὰ
ἁμαρτή ματα, καὶ ἱλαρῶς τὸ πρόσωπον ἐπαρεῖς εἰς τὸν οὐ ρανὸν, ἀκαταγνώστῳ
συνειδότι τὰς ἱκετείας ποιούμε νος· κἄν τι εὔξῃ καὶ ὑπόσχῃ τῷ Θεῷ, αὐτὸς ἐνισχύ σει
σε πρὸς πέρας ἀγαγεῖν τὰς πρὸς αὐτὸν ὑποσχέ σεις· αὐτὸς γάρ ἐστιν «ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν
ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ θέλειν καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν ὑπὲρ τῆς εὐδοκίας.» Ἀντὶ μέντοι τοῦ, «∆ώσει δέ
σοι ἀποδοῦναι τὰς εὐχὰς,» Θεοδοτίων, «Καὶ ὁριεῖς ῥῆμα, καὶ σταθήσεταί σοι,»
ἐξέδωκε· τουτέστιν, ἅπαν ὃ ἂν συντάξῃ καὶ τυπώσῃς, οὐ διαπεσεῖται· καὶ ἁπλῶς
εἰπεῖν, ἅπασάν σοι τὴν ἁρμόζουσαν δικαίῳ παρέξει διαγωγήν· καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ ὁδοί σου
κατευοδωθήσονται ὑπὸ τοῦ θείου ὁδηγούμε ναι φωτός· ἢ καὶ αἱ πράξεις σου λαμπραὶ
καὶ ἐπίδο ξοι ἔσονται. Ὅτι ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν, καὶ ἐρεῖς· Ὑπερηφανεύσατο. Ὡς μὲν
περὶ ἑτέρου δοκεῖ λέγειν· πρὸς δὲ τὸν Ἰὼβ ὁ λόγος. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο, φησὶν, ἔσται ταῦτα τῷ
μετανοοῦντι, ὅτι ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν, καὶ εἶπεν, ὅτι ἐνδίκως αὐτὸς ὑπέστη ἃ
πέπονθεν, ἐπειδὴ ὑπερη φανεύσατο. Καὶ κύφοντα ὀφθαλμοῖς σώσει. Τουτέστι τὸν τα
πεινόφρονα, τὸν κάτω βλέποντα διὰ τὸ δυσσυνείδητον καὶ ἀπαῤῥησίαστον, καθάπερ
ὁ ἐν τοῖς Εὐαγγελίοις δικαιωθεὶς τελώνης. ΚΕΦ. ΚΖʹ. Ἔτι δὲ προσθεὶς Ἰὼβ τῷ
προοιμίῳ εἶπεν. Ἔλαβεν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ Ἰὼβ ὁ διάβολος καὶ ἤτασεν αὐτὸν νυκτὸς καὶ
ἡμέρας· πρότερον μὲν διὰ τῶν ἐκτός· ὕστερον δὲ δι' αὐτοῦ τοῦ σώματος· μετὰ ταῦτα
καὶ διὰ τῶν φίλων. Ὅτε γὰρ αὐτὸν ἐδοκίμαζε διὰ τῆς γυναικὸς, καὶ οἶδεν, ὅτι οὐ
νενίκηται ὁ Ἰὼβ, τρεῖς φίλους ἤνεγκεν, οὐκ ἐχθροὺς, οὐκ ἐπίβουλα δόγματα
ἔχοντας· ἀλλ' ἀληθεῖς μὲν λόγους, οὐ καλῶς δὲ, οὐδὲ ἐν καιρῷ προσφερομένους· καὶ
ἐβούλετο διὰ τούτων ποιῆσαι τὸν δίκαιον φθέγξασθαί τι κατὰ τῆς Προ νοίας·
ἀσεβῆσαι διὰ τοὺς πόνους· ἐκκακῆσαι διὰ τὰς ἀλγηδόνας· ἀλλ' ὁ στεῤῥὸς ἀδάμας
οὗτος, ὅρα τί λέγει μετὰ τοὺς λόγους τῶν τριῶν, ὅτε ἐτέλεσε ὁ Ἐλιφὰζ τρεῖς
διαλέξεις, ὁ Βαλδὰδ τρεῖς, ὁ Σοφὰρ δύο. Οὐ γὰρ σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ ἄτοπα πράξας.
Τοῦτο καὶ Παῦλος ὕστερον ἐφθέγξατο, καὶ προσέθηκεν· «Ἀλλ' οὐκ ἐν τούτῳ
δεδικαίωμαι.» Πολλὴ ἡ παῤ ῥησία τοῦ δικαίου καὶ ἐπὶ τῷ προτέρῳ βίῳ, καὶ ἐπὶ τοῖς
κατὰ τὸν καιρὸν τῆς περιστάσεως, ὥστε αὐτὸν εἰπεῖν· Οὐδὲν ἐμαυτῷ σύνοιδα. ΚΕΦʹ.
ΚΘʹ. Ἁδροὶ δὲ ἐπαύσαντο λαλοῦντες. Ἢ κατὰ τὴν τῶν λοιπῶν ἔκδοσιν «οἱ
ἄρχοντες.» Οὗτοι παραχω 12.1041 ροῦντες τῷ δικαίῳ τοῦ λόγου, αὐτοὶ αὐτοῦ
παρόντος ἐσίγων. ∆άκτυλον ἐπιθέντες ἐπὶ τῷ στόματι. ∆όξει μὲν οὖν καὶ σημεῖον
εἶναι σιωπῆς τὸ, δάκτυλον ἐπιθεῖναι ἐπὶ τῷ στόματι· τάχα δὲ, ἐπεὶ ἡ χεὶρ ἀντὶ ἔργων
λαμβάνεται, δηλοῖ, ὅτι τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν ἐφίμου αὐτοῖς τὰ χείλη, καὶ οἱονεὶ δεσμός τις
τῷ στόματι ἐπέκειτο· ᾐσθήθησαν γὰρ, ὅτι οὐκ εἰσὶν ἄξιοι τοῦ λαλεῖν, παρόν τος τοῦ
Ἰὼβ, μείζονα ἔργα πεποιηκότος, αὐτοὶ ὀλίγα πεπραχότες· ὁ γὰρ δάκτυλος τὴν
ἐλαχίστην σημαίνει πρᾶξιν καὶ ἐνέργειαν. ∆ικαιοσύνην δὲ ἐνδεδύκειν. Καλὸν
χιτῶνα ὕφα νεν ἑαυτῷ ὁ Ἰὼβ, ἵνα ἐνδύσηται τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἀντὶ χιτῶνος. Ἴδε
αὐτοῦ καὶ τὸ ἱμάτιον· δικαιοσύνη ὁ χιτών· κρῖμα ἡ διπλοΐς. ΚΕΦ. ΛΒʹ.
orientation: Origen is expounding Eliphaz's speech in Job 22, applying its charges about stripping the naked and partiality to everyday Christian behavior, then turning to Job's own bold self-defense.
pass_a_gloss: If indeed someone has one tunic, and this tunic I strip off on the pretext of demanding what is mine, not having pitied that naked man, I have taken away the clothing of the naked. And many such things happen among us, whenever we lend, whenever we have debtors. Often our debtor is poor to excess, not able to repay; and we, having hardened our hearts, and not seeing that he feeds a wife and children, and barely feeds himself from the few obols procured for him, demand bitterly, sometimes even having more than enough by ourselves. These things therefore he says accusing Job, that, 'You took away the clothing of the naked.' Perhaps also he calls the not giving a garment to the naked a taking away; for he is a robber and a greedy person both the one not clothing the naked, and the one not feeding the one in need of bread. 'And you admired the faces of some.' This too is another sin; for it is a sin also to admire a face. So-and-so, because he is rich, I admire his face; but the poor man I trample down, since indeed he has no rank. 'Therefore the Almighty will be your helper.' A sound doctrine here Eliphaz speaks; for he supposes that Job suffers because of his sins, and that having endured he will be purified through the very suffering; and being purified, just as gold in a furnace, he is shown approved, having put off everything foreign, and having become unmixed with every evil. He says therefore, that, if you also endure what has befallen you, God will render you pure as silver refined by fire; and having become pure, you will have boldness, as having put off your sins, and cheerfully you will lift up your face to heaven, making your supplications with an uncondemned conscience; and if you vow and promise anything to God, he himself will strengthen you to bring to completion your promises to him; for he himself is 'the one working in us both the willing and the working for his good pleasure.' But instead of, 'And he will give you to repay your vows,' Theodotion published, 'And you will define a word, and it will be established for you'; that is, whatever you arrange and fix, it will not fall through; and to speak simply, he will provide you the whole way of life fitting for a righteous man; and all your ways will be prospered, being guided by the divine light; or also your deeds will be bright and distinguished. 'Because he humbled himself, and you will say: He acted proudly.' As about another he seems to speak; but the word is directed to Job. Because of this, he says, these things will be for the one who repents, because he humbled himself, and said, that justly he himself underwent what he suffered, since he acted proudly. 'And the one stooping with his eyes he will save.' That is, the humble-minded one, the one looking down because of his bad conscience and lack of boldness, just as the tax collector justified in the Gospels. CHAPTER 27. And still adding to his prologue Job said. The devil took authority over Job and tested him night and day; first through external things; later through the body itself; after these things also through his friends. For when he was testing him through his wife, and knew that Job has not been defeated, he brought three friends, not enemies, not having treacherous doctrines; but true words, yet not well, nor in season brought forward; and he wanted through these to make the righteous man utter something against Providence; to act impiously because of his pains; to lose heart because of his distresses; but this solid adamant, see what he says after the words of the three, when Eliphaz finished three speeches, Bildad three, Zophar two. 'For I am not conscious of having done wrong things.' This Paul also later uttered, and added: 'But not in this am I justified.' Great is the boldness of the righteous man both concerning his former life, and concerning the things at the time of his trial, so that he says: I am conscious of nothing against myself. CHAPTER 29. 'And the mighty ceased speaking.' Or according to the edition of the rest, 'the rulers.' These, yielding to the righteous man the word, themselves were silent when he was present. 'Having placed a finger on the mouth.' It will seem then also to be a sign of silence, to place a finger on the mouth; but perhaps, since the hand is taken for deeds, it shows that their work muzzled their lips, and as it were some bond lay upon their mouth; for they perceived that they are not worthy to speak, when Job was present, who had done greater works, while they had done little; for the finger signifies the smallest action and activity. 'And I had put on righteousness.' A beautiful tunic Job wove for himself, that he might put on righteousness instead of a tunic. See also his garment; righteousness is the tunic; judgment is the double cloak. CHAPTER 32.

choices.english: I have taken away the clothing of the naked
choices.why: Keeps the possessive force of the genitive and the perfect tense of the verb, matching the biblical citation Origen is expounding.
rejected: I stripped the naked of clothing
I robbed the naked of his garment

choices.english: having shut up our inward parts
choices.why: Renders the Greek idiom literally to preserve the bodily metaphor for closed compassion, which Origen uses to describe hard-hearted creditors.
Uses the fixed glossary rendering for παῤῥησία, which Origen presents as the reward of purification.
Preserves the metaphor of unbreakable metal for Job's endurance, which Origen uses to contrast with the friends' pressure.
Keeps the adjective 'mighty' as the primary reading while noting the variant 'rulers' in the gloss, matching Origen's own comment on the alternative editions.
rejected: And the great men fell silent

choices.english: And I had put on righteousness
choices.why: Renders the pluperfect to show Job's completed act of clothing himself in virtue, which Origen then elaborates as a woven tunic.
rejected: And I was clothed in righteousness

pass_b_english: But if someone has a single tunic, and I strip that tunic from him on the pretext of demanding what is mine, without pitying the naked man, then I have taken away the clothing of the naked. Many such things happen among us when we lend money and when we have debtors. Often our debtor is extremely poor and cannot repay. We harden our hearts and do not see that he feeds a wife and children and barely feeds himself from the few small coins he earns, yet we demand payment bitterly, sometimes even while we have more than enough at home. So Eliphaz says this in accusing Job: "You took away the clothing of the naked" (Job 22:6). Perhaps he also calls the failure to give a garment to the naked an act of taking away, for the one who does not clothe the naked and the one who does not feed the one in need of bread is a robber and a greedy person.

"And you admired the faces of some" (Job 22:8). This is another sin, for admiring a face is also a sin. A certain person is rich, and I admire his face, but I trample down the poor man because he has no rank.

"So the Almighty will be your helper" (Job 22:25). Here Eliphaz speaks a sound doctrine, for he thinks Job suffers because of his sins, and that by enduring he will be purified through the suffering itself. And being purified, like gold in a furnace, he is shown to be genuine, having cast off everything foreign and become unmixed with every evil. He says, then, that if you also endure what has happened to you, God will give you back pure, like silver refined by fire. And when you have become pure, you will have boldness, since you have cast off your sins, and you will lift your face cheerfully to heaven, making your supplications with an uncondemned conscience, and so with boldness. And if you vow and promise anything to God, he himself will strengthen you to bring your promises to him to completion, for he is "the one working in us both to will and to work for his good pleasure" (Philippians 2:13). Instead of "He will give you to repay your vows" (Job 22:27), Theodotion rendered it, "And you will determine a word, and it will be established for you," that is, whatever you arrange and set in order will not fail. To put it simply, he will provide you with the whole way of life that befits a righteous person, and all your paths will prosper, guided by the divine light; or your deeds will be bright and successful.

"Because he humbled himself, and you will say: He acted proudly" (Job 22:29). He seems to speak about someone else, but the word is directed at Job. For this reason, he says, these things will happen to the one who repents: because he humbled himself and said that he justly underwent what he suffered, since he had acted proudly. "And he will save the one who bows down with his eyes" (Job 22:29). That is, the humble-minded one, the one who looks down because of a troubled conscience and lack of boldness, like the tax collector who was justified in the Gospels.

Chapter 27. And Job, adding still more to his opening speech, said: The devil received authority over Job and tested him night and day, first through external things, then through his own body, and after these things also through his friends. For when he tested him through his wife and saw that Job had not been defeated, he brought three friends, not enemies, not men holding treacherous doctrines, but men with true words that were not offered well or at the right time. Through them he wanted to make the righteous man say something against Providence, to act impiously because of his pains, to lose heart because of his anguish. But this solid adamant, see what he says after the speeches of the three, when Eliphaz had finished three discourses, Bildad three, and Zophar two: "For I am not conscious of having done anything wrong" (Job 27:6). Paul later uttered this too, and added: "But I am not justified by this" (1 Corinthians 4:4). Great is the boldness of the righteous man, both concerning his former life and concerning the things at the time of his trial, so that he says: "I am conscious of nothing against myself."

Chapter 29. "And the mighty ceased speaking" (Job 29:9). Or according to the other Greek translations, "the rulers." These men, yielding the word to the righteous man, fell silent in his presence. "Putting a finger on their mouth" (Job 29:9). It may seem that putting a finger on the mouth is a sign of silence. But perhaps, since the hand is taken for deeds, it shows that their work muzzled their lips, and a kind of bond lay upon their mouth. For they perceived that they were not worthy to speak while Job was present, since he had done greater deeds while they had accomplished little. For the finger signifies the smallest action and activity.

"And I had put on righteousness" (Job 29:14). Job wove a beautiful tunic for himself, so that he might put on righteousness instead of a tunic. See also his cloak: righteousness is the tunic, judgment is the double cloak. Chapter 32. [The commentary on chapters 30–31 is lost.]

problems.why: Variant translations of same Hebrew term presented without clarity.

problems.quote: But if someone has a single tunic, and I strip that tunic from him
problems.why: Abrupt shift to first person without clear speaker—author? Job? Eliphaz?
problems.fix: Clarify this is author illustrating Eliphaz's accusation.

problems.quote: we shut up our inward parts and do not see
problems.why: Literal rendering of Greek 'splagchna' as 'inward parts' obscures meaning of compassion.
problems.fix: Use 'hearts' or 'we close up our compassion'.

problems.quote: So-and-so is rich, and I admire his face
problems.why: Colloquial 'So-and-so' sounds flippant for serious moral discussion.
The verse 'Because he humbled himself, and you will say: He acted proudly' does not match standard Job 22:29; seems conflated or misremembered.

polish.changed: Clarified the speaker of the opening first-person example as Origen's own moral illustration, identified Theodotion as another Greek translator, replaced the obscure 'inward parts' with 'hearts,' removed the flippant 'So-and-so,' explained 'adamant' as Job's firmness, and clarified that 'the other editions' refers to other Greek translations.

notes.why: Variant translations of same Hebrew term presented without clarity.
Ancient translator mentioned without any explanation of who he was.
notes.fix: Add note: 'Theodotion, 2nd-c. Greek translator of Hebrew Bible.'

notes.quote: But if someone has a single tunic, and I strip that tunic from him
notes.why: Abrupt shift to first person without clear speaker—author? Job? Eliphaz?
notes.fix: Clarify this is author illustrating Eliphaz's accusation.

notes.quote: we shut up our inward parts and do not see
notes.why: Literal rendering of Greek 'splagchna' as 'inward parts' obscures meaning of compassion.
notes.fix: Use 'hearts' or 'we close up our compassion'.

notes.quote: So-and-so is rich, and I admire his face
notes.why: Colloquial 'So-and-so' sounds flippant for serious moral discussion.
The verse 'Because he humbled himself, and you will say: He acted proudly' does not match standard Job 22:29; seems conflated or misremembered.
notes.fix: Verify against Hebrew text; may need note on variant reading.

variants.text: those who came to visit him

notes.why: Bildad and the friends are called by different labels that obscure identity.
notes.fix: Use 'Bildad the Shuhite' and 'Job's friends' consistently.

notes.why: Satan, dragon, devil, and 'the proud one' are the same figure but named differently.
notes.fix: Note once that dragon = Satan = the devil and use one term consistently.

notes.why: Theodotion is named without explanation of who he was.
notes.fix: Add: Theodotion was a Greek translator of the Old Testament.

notes.why: 'Adamant' as metaphor for Job's firmness is obscure to modern readers.
notes.fix: Add: 'adamant' = an unbreakable hard substance, here meaning Job's resolve.

notes.quote: we shut up our inward parts
notes.why: 'Inward parts' for lack of compassion is an odd literal rendering; likely means 'we harden our hearts.'
notes.fix: Render as 'we harden our hearts' or 'we close our compassion.'

notes.why: Refers to other Greek translations of Job without explaining what editions these are.
notes.fix: Add: 'other editions' = other Greek translations of the Old Testament.

polish.changed: Clarified the opening moral application as Origen's own voice, removed the redundant gloss about Theodotion, and unified the variant rendering of "the rulers" so readers do not mistake it for a different group.

notes.why: Same Greek word translated two ways in same verse discussion; reader thinks different groups.

notes.quote: Theodotion, another Greek translator of the Old Testament
notes.why: Theodotion never introduced before; reader doesn't know who he is or why he matters.
notes.fix: Footnote identifying Theodotion (2nd c. CE Greek translator).

notes.quote: But if someone has a single tunic
notes.why: Shift from Eliphaz's accusation to author's moral application without transition; 'I' is suddenly the preacher.
notes.fix: Add transition like 'We too must consider'.

last_rejected.quote: and you will lift your face cheerfully to heaven, making your supplications with an uncondemned conscience.
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ ἱλαρῶς τὸ πρόσωπον ἐπαρεῖς εἰς τὸν οὐ ρανὸν, ἀκαταγνώστῳ συνειδότι τὰς ἱκετείας ποιούμε νος
last_rejected.why: Source says 'lift your face cheerfully to heaven'; English omits 'lift your face' (ἐπαρεῖς τὸ πρόσωπον).
last_rejected.fix: and you will lift your face cheerfully to heaven, making your supplications with an uncondemned conscience.
last_rejected.ruling: English has 'lift your face cheerfully to heaven'; ἐπαρεῖς τὸ πρόσωπον is rendered as 'lift your face'.

last_rejected.quote: So Eliphaz says this in accusing Job
last_rejected.source_quote: Ταῦτα οὖν λέγει ἐγκαλῶν τῷ Ἰὼβ
last_rejected.why: Source says 'he says' without naming Eliphaz; English adds name not in text.
last_rejected.fix: So he says this in accusing Job
last_rejected.ruling: Context makes Eliphaz clear; supplying the name is normal translation practice, not an error.

last_rejected.quote: without pitying the naked man
last_rejected.why: Greek is aorist participle 'not having pitied,' not present 'without pitying.'
last_rejected.fix: not having pitied that naked man
last_rejected.ruling: 'Without pitying' adequately renders aorist participle μὴ ἐλεήσας; no meaning is lost.

last_rejected.quote: I have taken away
last_rejected.why: Greek is first person singular aorist middle, but context is general condition, not autobiographical.
last_rejected.fix: one has taken away
last_rejected.ruling: First-person ἀφειλόμην is correctly translated 'I have taken away'; the conditional is rhetorical.

last_rejected.quote: we shut up our inward parts
last_rejected.why: Greek means 'having closed/locked up our inward parts (compassion),' not 'shut up' as silence.
last_rejected.fix: having locked up our compassion
last_rejected.ruling: 'Shut up our inward parts' correctly renders ἀποκλείσαντες τὰ σπλάγχνα; no real error.

last_rejected.quote: the failure to give a garment to the naked an act of taking away
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ μὴ δοῦναι τῷ γυμνῷ ἱμάτιον ἀφαίρεσιν ὀνομάζει
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'he calls... a taking away,' not 'an act of taking away.'
last_rejected.fix: he calls the failure to give a garment to the naked a taking away
last_rejected.ruling: 'An act of taking away' is a natural English rendering of ἀφαίρεσιν; no meaning is lost.

last_rejected.quote: a robber and a greedy person
last_rejected.why: Greek has two distinct terms; 'robber' is too strong for ἀποστερητής (defrauder/one who deprives).
last_rejected.fix: a defrauder and a greedy person
last_rejected.ruling: ἀποστερητής can mean 'robber'; within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: So-and-so is rich
last_rejected.why: Greek uses 'ὁ δεῖνα' (so-and-so) as generic example, but English loses the contemptuous indefinite force.
last_rejected.fix: So-and-so, because he is rich
last_rejected.ruling: 'So-and-so' correctly renders ὁ δεῖνα; the claim is a mere preference.

last_rejected.quote: he is shown to be genuine
last_rejected.why: Greek is passive 'is shown to be tested/approved,' not middle 'shows himself.'
last_rejected.fix: he is shown to be approved
last_rejected.ruling: 'Is shown to be genuine' correctly renders δόκιμος ἀποφαίνεται; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: God will give you back pure
last_rejected.why: Greek means 'will render/restore you pure,' not 'give you back.'
last_rejected.fix: God will render you pure
last_rejected.ruling: 'Give you back pure' adequately renders ἀποδώσει σε καθαρὸν; no major error.

last_rejected.quote: he himself will strengthen you to bring your promises to him to completion
last_rejected.source_quote: αὐτὸς ἐνισχύσει σε πρὸς πέρας ἀγαγεῖν τὰς πρὸς αὐτὸν ὑποσχέσεις
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'he will strengthen you to bring to completion the promises to him,' not 'your promises.'
last_rejected.fix: he himself will strengthen you to bring to completion the promises to him
last_rejected.ruling: 'Your promises to him' correctly translates τὰς πρὸς αὐτὸν ὑποσχέσεις; claim is a preference.

last_rejected.quote: And you will determine a word, and it will be established for you
last_rejected.source_quote: Καὶ ὁριεῖς ῥῆμα, καὶ σταθήσεταί σοι
last_rejected.why: Theodotion's Greek uses future indicative, but English loses the authoritative 'decree/command' sense of ὁριεῖς.
last_rejected.fix: And you will decree a word, and it will stand for you
last_rejected.ruling: 'Determine a word' captures ὁριεῖς adequately; no meaning is lost.

last_rejected.quote: your deeds will be bright and successful
last_rejected.source_quote: αἱ πράξεις σου λαμπραὶ καὶ ἐπίδοξοι ἔσονται
last_rejected.why: Greek 'ἐπίδοξοι' means 'glorious/splendid,' not 'successful.'
last_rejected.fix: your deeds will be bright and glorious
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπίδοξοι can mean 'successful' or 'splendid'; within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: Because he humbled himself, and you will say: He acted proudly
last_rejected.source_quote: Ὅτι ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν, καὶ ἐρεῖς· Ὑπερηφανεύσατο
last_rejected.why: Greek is third person 'he humbled himself... he acted proudly,' but English splits subjects confusingly.
last_rejected.fix: Because he humbled himself, and you will say, He acted proudly
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly preserves third-person subjects; the colon separates the quotation. No error.

last_rejected.quote: the one who looks down because of a troubled conscience and lack of boldness
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸν κάτω βλέποντα διὰ τὸ δυσσυνείδητον καὶ ἀπαῤῥησίαστον
last_rejected.why: Greek nouns are neuter substantives 'the conscience-stricken and boldness-lacking state,' not abstract descriptions.
last_rejected.fix: the one who looks down because of conscience-stricken and boldness-lacking condition
last_rejected.ruling: 'Troubled conscience and lack of boldness' correctly renders the neuter substantives; no error.

last_rejected.quote: not men holding treacherous doctrines
last_rejected.why: Greek 'ἐπίβουλα' means 'plotting/insidious,' not 'treacherous' in doctrinal sense.
last_rejected.fix: not men holding insidious doctrines
last_rejected.ruling: 'Treacherous' is within the normal range for ἐπίβουλα; not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: to lose heart
last_rejected.why: Greek means 'to give up/faint/turn coward,' stronger than 'lose heart.'
last_rejected.fix: to give up
last_rejected.ruling: 'Lose heart' is a standard rendering of ἐκκακῆσαι; no meaning is lost.

last_rejected.quote: this solid adamant
last_rejected.why: Greek has demonstrative 'this' before adjective, but 'solid adamant' is awkward; 'adamant' alone is the term.
last_rejected.fix: this unyielding adamant
last_rejected.ruling: 'Solid adamant' correctly renders στερεὸς ἀδάμας; the claim is a mere preference.

last_rejected.quote: I am not conscious of having done anything wrong
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ γὰρ σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ ἄτοπα πράξας
last_rejected.why: Greek 'ἄτοπα' means 'out of place/improper,' not 'wrong' in moral sense.
last_rejected.fix: For I am not conscious to myself of having done anything improper
last_rejected.ruling: ἄτοπα πράξας means 'done anything wrong'; within normal range, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: But I am not justified by this
last_rejected.why: Greek is perfect passive 'I have not been justified,' not present 'I am not justified.'
last_rejected.fix: But in this I have not been justified
last_rejected.ruling: English present passive 'I am not justified' adequately renders the perfect δεδικαίωμαι; no major error.

last_rejected.quote: the mighty ceased speaking
last_rejected.why: Greek 'ἁδροί' means 'stout/great ones,' but LXX variant is 'οἱ ἄρχοντες' (rulers).
last_rejected.fix: And the great ones ceased speaking
last_rejected.ruling: ἁδροί can mean 'mighty'; the translation notes the variant. Not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: yielding the word to the righteous man
last_rejected.why: Greek genitive 'τοῦ λόγου' means 'yielding the word/right of speech,' not 'yielding the word to.'
last_rejected.fix: yielding the right of speech to the righteous man
last_rejected.ruling: 'Yielding the word to the righteous man' correctly renders παραχωροῦντες τῷ δικαίῳ τοῦ λόγου.

last_rejected.quote: their work muzzled their lips
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ ἔργον αὐτῶν ἐφίμου αὐτοῖς τὰ χείλη
last_rejected.why: Greek is singular 'work,' but English pluralizes; 'ἐφίμου' is imperfect 'was muzzling,' not simple past.
last_rejected.fix: their work was muzzling their lips
last_rejected.ruling: Singular/plural and tense differences here do not change meaning; not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: the smallest action and activity
last_rejected.why: Greek singular article with two nouns asyndetically, 'the smallest deed and activity.'
last_rejected.fix: the smallest deed and activity
last_rejected.ruling: 'The smallest action and activity' correctly renders the Greek; the claim is a mere preference.

last_rejected.quote: Job wove a beautiful tunic for himself
last_rejected.source_quote: Καλὸν χιτῶνα ὕφανεν ἑαυτῷ ὁ Ἰὼβ
last_rejected.why: Greek word order emphasizes 'a beautiful tunic,' with 'for himself' as dative of advantage.
last_rejected.fix: Job wove for himself a beautiful tunic
last_rejected.ruling: Word order and dative are correctly translated; the claim is a mere preference.

last_rejected.quote: the one working in us both to will and to work
last_rejected.source_quote: ὁ ἐνεργῶν ἐν ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ θέλειν καὶ τὸ ἐνεργεῖν
last_rejected.why: Glossary term 'boldness' for παῤῥησία appears earlier correctly, but check consistency.
last_rejected.fix: no change needed
last_rejected.ruling: The English correctly renders the Philippians quotation; no glossary or consistency error exists.

last_rejected.quote: And Job, adding still more to his opening speech, said: The devil received authority over Job
last_rejected.source_quote: Ἔτι δὲ προσθεὶς Ἰὼβ τῷ προοιμίῳ εἶπεν. Ἔλαβεν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ Ἰὼβ ὁ διάβολος
last_rejected.why: The colon presents Origen's comment as words Job himself speaks.
last_rejected.fix: And Job, adding still to his opening words, said: The devil received authority over Job and tested him night and day.
last_rejected.ruling: The source has a full stop after εἶπεν. The English colon is a minor punctuation choice. 'Ἔλαβεν ἐξουσίαν τοῦ Ἰὼβ ὁ διάβολος' speaks of Job in the third person, so no reader would take it as Job's own words.
